name: libvips
workload: Load a 10,000 x 10,000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 px off every edge, shrink by 10% with bilinear interpolation, sharpen with a 3x3 convolution, save again; quickest real time of five runs, peak RSS sampled with ps.
claimed_speedup: vips-c 8.18: 0.57 s, 94.28 MB peak vs ImageMagick convert 7.1.1: 4.44 s, 1499.29 MB (7.79x slower, ~16x more memory). Other rows on the same page: GraphicsMagick gm 1.4 2.05 s, pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s, OpenCV 4.10 3.15 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; the page says systems were used 'as packaged for Ubuntu' (distribution binaries of libvips 8.18 and ImageMagick 7.1.1).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025
tradeoffs: Demand-driven streaming pipeline with a C API (also a C++ binding vips8 in the repo); LGPL linking rules apply. Multi-threaded by default. Not a drop-in for ImageMagick command lines.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (the libvips author's own wiki and vips-bench repo, code public but no compiler flags, distro packages). The page itself says the test 'does a lot of file IO and relatively little processing, which flatters libvips' and that single-threaded tools like Pillow and OpenCV are penalised on a 16-core machine. The workload is mostly TIFF I/O plus a bilinear shrink and 3x3 sharpen, so it measures a pipeline rather than a pure resampling kernel. libvips's single-thread row (1thr-vips-c 0.77 s) is still about 5.7x faster than ImageMagick (derived from page data).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SIMD image resize library C++ faster than ImageMagick benchmark site:github.com' surfaced the libvips wiki 'Speed and memory use' page

name: zimg
workload: Time in ms to resize a FHD frame to UHD with the Lanczos filter (swscale flags scale=3840:2160:sws_flags=lanczos+accurate_rnd:sws_dither=none), and to convert a FHD frame from BT.709 YUV to BT.2020 (swscale colorspace filter, format yuv420p10).
claimed_speedup: Lanczos FHD->UHD resize: 7.7 ms vs 15.2 ms (Core i7-8565U), 10.8 ms vs 22.2 ms (Xeon Platinum 8176). BT.709 -> BT.2020 conversion: 8.3 ms vs 17.5 ms (i7-8565U), 11.5 ms vs 25.6 ms (Xeon 8176). About 2x on each row (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U and Intel Xeon Platinum 8176
tradeoffs: C++17 library covering scaling, colorspace conversion (Rec.709, Rec.2020, SMPTE-C, BT.2020 constant luminance) and depth conversion with dithering; designed to be thread-safe with allocation and I/O separated from processing. The README says it is optimized for Intel architecture. Not a colour management system (no drastic gamut reduction). Autotools is the supported build system.
caveats: README numbers only: no benchmark harness in the repo, no compiler or flags, no frame content or thread count. Compares against an old swscale (4.0.2) and zimg 2.8, so numbers are likely several years old; swscale has had x86 improvements since. WTFPL is a permissive public-domain-style licence not on the OSI list, so verify before copying code.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'swscale vs libyuv vs zimg benchmark RGB to YUV conversion speed comparison repository' (github.com only) surfaced the zimg README Performance section

name: yuv2rgb (descampsa)
workload: YUV420p to RGB24 and RGB24 to YUV420p conversion of a 4K (4096x2160) image, 100 iterations, using the repo's test_yuv_rgb program; SSE2 versions, a plain C version, FFmpeg swscale and Intel IPP are timed side by side.
claimed_speedup: yuv2rgb, 100 iterations: sse2_aligned 0.607 s and sse2_unaligned 0.704 s vs ffmpeg 1.227 s / 1.221 s (about 2x). rgb2yuv: sse2_aligned 0.641 s and sse2_unaligned 0.677 s vs ffmpeg 3.398 s / 3.386 s (about 5.3x). Plain C std path 2.63 s / 2.59 s. Intel IPP 9.0.1 is slightly faster than the SSE2 code (0.636 s yuv2rgb, 0.579-0.594 s rgb2yuv).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9.2, swscale 3.0.0, IPP 9.0.1; built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release plus -Werror -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -std=c99 from CMakeLists.txt (no explicit -O or -msse flags in the file)
tradeoffs: Small C99 library: only YUV420p <-> RGB24 (plus a few color-space matrices); aligned and unaligned SSE2 variants; no AVX2 or NEON. Author calls it an exercise in learning SSE intrinsics.
caveats: Author's own run on one laptop CPU with an old swscale 3.0.0 (MMX path, per the README); modern swscale has AVX2 paths and would narrow the gap. Intel IPP beat it slightly. Tier A rests on public test program, stated compiler and CPU and the documented Release build; flags are the CMake Release preset, not spelled out. Inputs are a single image run 100 times (cache-warm).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'swscale vs libyuv vs zimg benchmark RGB to YUV conversion speed comparison repository' surfaced descampsa/yuv2rgb

name: sparkyuv
workload: Google Benchmark timings of 8-bit and 10-bit RGBA <-> YCbCr (4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0), NV12/NV21, premultiply and unpremultiply, sparkyuv vs libyuv; image size not stated in the README.
claimed_speedup: 10-bit YCbCr 4:2:0 to RGBA: 569,507 ns vs libyuv 1,090,866 ns (about 1.9x). 8-bit YCbCr 4:2:2 to RGBA: 346,422 ns vs 458,754 ns (about 1.3x); 4:4:4: 332,122 vs 365,939 ns. Unpremultiply: 895,136 ns vs 1,382,779 ns. Slower rows: RGBA8 to YCbCr420 543,371 ns vs libyuv 270,961 ns; Premultiply 259,198 ns vs libyuv 213,810 ns. NV12 decode essentially tied (386,739 vs 387,258 ns).
hardware: Apple M3 Pro (12 cores; Google Benchmark header shows 24 MHz nominal clock)
tradeoffs: Supports many YUV matrices (YCgCo, YIQ, YDbDr, constant-luminance), 8/10/12-bit, 22 SIMD targets. Chroma-subsampled encode uses a fixed bilinear downscale that cannot be turned off.
caveats: Mixed result: the README itself says 8-bit decode is 'very close to libyuv' and that libyuv is faster at 8-bit YCbCr encode. Win is mostly on 10/12-bit and on arm64 NEON; the README says on other platforms it 'should be considered same'. Benchmark source is in tools/YuvBenchmarkMain.cpp but compiler and flags are not stated and no x86 numbers are given. Repo archived by owner 10 Feb 2025; GitHub licence label lists Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'swscale vs libyuv vs zimg ...' surfaced awxkee/sparkyuv; github.com/topics/yuv?l=c%2B%2B listed it

name: xxYUV
workload: RGB to YUV encode and YUV to RGB decode (YU12/YV12 and NV12/NV21) timed in microseconds on an unstated frame size, using the benchmark harness in the xxImGui experimental branch; xxYUV vs libyuv vs Apple Accelerate on macOS (M1 and x86) and on an i7-8700B.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1 NEON: encode YU12/YV12 37 us vs libyuv 48 us, decode YU12/YV12 38 us vs 122 us, decode NV12/NV21 42 us vs 89 us. i7-8700B AVX2: encode YU12/YV12 31 us vs 48 us, encode NV12/NV21 33 us vs 39 us, decode YU12/YV12 46 us vs 60 us, decode NV12/NV21 39 us vs 54 us. On the M1 machine, SSSE3 encode 134 us vs libyuv 146 us.
hardware: Apple M1 (rows labelled AMX, NEON, SSSE3, SSE2) and Intel i7-8700B (rows labelled AVX2, SSSE3, SSE2)
tradeoffs: Small RGB<->YUV conversion library with SSE2, SSSE3, AVX2, NEON and Apple AMX paths; far narrower format coverage than libyuv; no scaling.
caveats: First-party table only: frame size, compiler and flags are not stated, and the harness lives in a different repository (xxImGui, 'experimental' branch) that I did not open. Last commit is from October 2021, so the libyuv version compared is old. Tier C.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'swscale vs libyuv vs zimg benchmark RGB to YUV conversion speed comparison repository' surfaced metarutaiga/xxYUV

name: Little-CMS fast_float plugin
workload: RawTherapee exporting a 45.6 MP image to full-size JPEG with the RTv4_sRGB output profile, timing the Lab-to-RGB output colour transform (lab2rgbOut) with and without the fast_float plugin.
claimed_speedup: lab2rgbOut 5312 ms without the fast-float plugin vs 754 ms with it (about 7x). The plugin's PDF also states increased throughput for 8-bit gray/RGB/CMYK transforms and for 32-bit float transforms.
stars_or_usage: 751 stars (Little-CMS repo); shipped in lcms2 since 2.10 and used by RawTherapee
tradeoffs: The plugin lives in plugins/fast_float of the lcms2 repo and registers optimized float-to-float and 8-bit transform kernels (SIMD where available). Only Gray, RGB, CMYK and Lab are optimizable, transforms must have fixed formats (no cmsChangeBuffersFormat), and big blocks are needed to amortise startup.
caveats: Numbers come from a RawTherapee developer's comment in an issue, not a controlled benchmark: no CPU, thread count, compiler or flags. The plugin is GPL-3.0 (a commercial alternative licence is offered by the author) while the lcms2 core is MIT, hence 'mixed'. The plugin ships a testbed (plugins/fast_float/testbed/fast_float_testbed.c) that prints MPixel/sec, which would let someone reproduce it, but I found no published numbers from it. The baseline is lcms2 itself, not a different library.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'lcms2 fast_float plugin faster than Little CMS benchmark github' surfaced RawTherapee issue #6016

name: RGB2Y
workload: RGB (BGR) image to 8-bit grayscale conversion with OpenCV's default weights; main.cpp runs 50 warmups and 100 timed runs against cv::cvtColor and prints microseconds.
claimed_speedup: Roughly 3x faster than OpenCV's implementation with AVX2, or 2x faster with SSE only (repo description: 2-4x faster than OpenCV).
tradeoffs: Header-only (RGB2Y.h), AVX2 or SSE only, no NEON; single operation (RGB to gray) with equal or OpenCV-default weights; the author says SSE is about 50% slower than AVX2.
caveats: Claim is a single README sentence with no numbers, CPU, compiler or flags; the demo harness (main.cpp) is public and prints per-run timings but I did not run it. Written against a 2018-era OpenCV (uses CV_BGR2GRAY constant), so a modern OpenCV with universal intrinsics may be closer. Last commit March 2021 (adding a LICENSE file); code last updated 29 Sep 2018.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'OpenCV cvtColor slower SIMD RGB to grayscale BGR to YUV AVX2 NEON library benchmark C++ github cvtColor' (github.com) surfaced komrad36/RGB2Y

name: H264Sharp (native SIMD color converter)
workload: 1080p RGB -> YUV and YUV -> RGB conversion, 5000 iterations, with a custom thread pool, at 1 to 16 threads, H264Sharp native converter vs OpenCV.
claimed_speedup: Ryzen 7 3700X: 1 thread 11919 ms (OpenCV) vs 4899 ms; 4 threads 3807 vs 1303 ms; 8 threads 2543 vs 822 ms; 16 threads 2462 vs 824 ms. Intel i7 10600U: 1 thread 11719 vs 6010 ms; 8 threads 3560 vs 1839 ms. README headline: up to 2.9x faster than OpenCV (the 8-thread Ryzen row works out to about 3.1x, derived from page data).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X desktop and Intel i7 10600U laptop (as written in the README)
tradeoffs: The repo is a .NET wrapper around Cisco OpenH264 whose native C++ folder H264SharpNative contains the RGB/YUV converters (Rgb2YuvAVX2.cpp, Yuv2RgbAVX2.cpp, SSE and NEON variants, thread pool); extracting just the converter for C++ use means taking those files. Formats are YUV <-> RGB/BGR/RGBA/BGRA only.
caveats: Benchmark code is not in the repo, compiler and flags are not stated, and the OpenCV version and thread configuration (OpenCV's own threading vs the custom thread pool) are not described. Primary language is C#; the C++ converter is a component. Last commit March 2025.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/rgb2yuv page listed ReferenceType/H264Sharp; README 'Converter Bechmarks' section

name: FastResize (fast_resize)
workload: Batch-resize 1,000 images per format to 800 px width, JPEG quality 85 output, 2 runs averaged; JPG 1179x1409, PNG 2104x1160, BMP 1045x1045, WEBP 4275x2451.
claimed_speedup: JPG: 2.10 s vs libvips (parallel) 5.24 s vs imageflow 6.60 s; PNG: 3.43 s vs 6.18 s vs 8.41 s; BMP: 1.65 s vs 4.72 s; WEBP: 14.03 s vs 23.52 s vs 15.69 s. README: up to 2.9x faster than libvips, 3.1x faster than imageflow, 3-4x less RAM (JPG peak 271 MB vs libvips 460 MB).
hardware: MacBook Pro M2, 16 GB, macOS Sonoma
tradeoffs: C++14 core with CLI and Ruby gem; decodes via libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp and stb_image; resizing is done by stb_image_resize2 (Mitchell, Catmull-Rom, Box, Triangle filters) with a thread pool and memory-mapped I/O. Only these filters; no Lanczos listed.
caveats: The resampling kernel is stb_image_resize2 (stb is the listed baseline), so the gain is from batch threading, libjpeg-turbo decode and avoiding per-image process start, not a faster resize kernel. Baseline libvips was driven through its vips CLI (one process per image is plausible but not stated), so process start-up may dominate; libvips sequential rows are far slower still. Benchmark commands are not published, one machine, two runs, no compiler flags. Repo is new (first commit Dec 2025, latest Jan 2026) with 21 commits. 'Fastest on the planet' is marketing language.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch '"faster than stb_image_resize" image resizing library' surfaced tranhuucanh/fast_resize

name: libyuv
workload: YUV/RGB format conversion and scaling (ARGB, I420, NV12 and others) in video and imaging pipelines.
claimed_speedup: No numbers on pages I opened. The libheif issue cites an ffmpeg-devel thread saying libyuv 'performs better than libswscale'; in the same issue a YUV420 HEVC multi-tile decode to interleaved RGB took 42 ms with the ffmpeg decoder plugin plus libheif's own yuv2rgb conversion vs 30 ms with the ffmpeg decoder plugin plus libyuv for the conversion (whole-step times, not the conversion alone).
stars_or_usage: 930 stars on this unofficial GitHub mirror (upstream is the Chromium project libyuv)
tradeoffs: Optimized for SSSE3/AVX2 on x86, Neon/SVE2/SME on Arm, MSA on MIPS and RVV on RISC-V; conversion, scaling, rotation. Official upstream is chromium.googlesource.com/libyuv/libyuv; the GitHub repo is an unofficial mirror (issues and PRs go upstream).
caveats: Evidence is thin: the libswscale comparison comes from an ffmpeg-devel mailing-list thread that the sandbox blocks (a search snippet reported about 4.19 s for libswscale vs 0.93 s for libyuv scaling 1088x1920 BGR24 to 480x854 YUV420P 500 times on an Intel Core i5 MacBook Pro, and 5-10x on an Apple M1 for RGBA to YUV420P, snippet only and unverified). The libheif numbers compare against libheif's own converter, not swscale. The incumbent role is better evidenced from sparkyuv and xxYUV, which both benchmark against libyuv and are faster only in some rows. Recorded as tier D because libyuv is clearly notable; a verifier with access to the ffmpeg-devel thread could upgrade it.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'libyuv github scale convert ARGB I420 performance faster than libswscale benchmark' surfaced libheif issue #1215; repo page github.com/lemenkov/libyuv
